performers: Chorale Philippe Caillard; Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo, Louis Frémaux
intro: The Agnus Dei is the fifth movement of Fauré’s Requiem, Op. 48. The tenors sing the text over a separate melody in the violas; the choir then returns to the music of the work’s opening, and the viola melody comes back to end the movement.

sections.label: A′ · Tenor melody returns
sections.mNote: The tenor melody returns over the separate string melody.

D · Introit theme returns, D minor
A″ · Strings alone in D major
sections.mNote: The opening string melody returns a minor third lower.

relations.label: The instrumental melody returns lower
relations.basis: The instrumental close recalls the opening string melody after the Introit quotation, as described in the listening notes. The measured shift is three semitones down, consistent with the opening F-major material returning in D major. CENS diagonal mean 0.912, sustained 18.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift -3 semitones and time offset 320 s (cache/form/faure-requiem-agnus-dei.txt, candidate 3; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Opening melody, violins and violas
cues.text: Violins and violas begin an F major melody. After six instrumental bars the tenors enter with a different melody above it. The violas continue their line, and the basses play plucked notes underneath.
cues.evidence: Fauré, Requiem, Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 70–73: six instrumental bars precede the tenor entry. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/4c/IMSLP30151-PMLP21398-Faure-Op048fs.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recording, Monaco, 1962
cues.text: Louis Frémaux and the orchestra recorded the Requiem in Monaco in August 1962. According to the Erato sleeve, the recording took place in the cathedral on 11 August. Canon Henri Carol played the organ.
cues.evidence: Erato LDE 3228 sleeve (Internet Archive scan): “Enregistré en la Cathédrale N.-D. de l’Immaculée Conception, à Monaco, le 11 Août 1962”; organist Chanoine Henri Carol; direction Louis Frémaux. https://archive.org/details/faure-o-requiem-cantique-de-jean-racine-louis-fremaux

cues.title: Full choir enters
cues.text: The other voices join the tenors, and the harmony moves towards the minor. The choral chords change chromatically against the melody in the violas and cellos. The strings keep the same walking pace beneath.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 74–77: full choral petition over the continuing lower-string melody, with chromatic changes in the choral parts.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the tenor melody
cues.text: The tenors sing the prayer alone again. F major returns with them, and the violas resume their flowing melody. The other voices rest.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 77–80: the tenor melody returns with the other choral staves silent.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Soprano C on “Lux”
cues.text: The sopranos hold C on “Lux”. The other voices enter beneath it in six parts, and the same note becomes the third of an A♭ major chord.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 80–81: soprano C and the six-part choral entry at rehearsal E, with A♭ in the bass.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, Madeleine, 1888
cues.text: On 16 January 1888 Fauré conducted the first version of the Requiem at the Madeleine in Paris, for the funeral of the architect Joseph Lesoufaché. It had five movements. The Offertoire and Libera me were added later.
cues.evidence: Première and revision history, with references to Jean-Michel Nectoux and Jessica Duchen: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Requiem_(Faur%C3%A9)

cues.title: Philippe Fauré on the Requiem
cues.text: Fauré’s elder son Philippe wrote that his father composed the Requiem “between two bereavements”. He added that the luceat eis is surely murmured for those who rocked Fauré as a child, and whom Fauré would like to rock in the mysterious beyond.
cues.evidence: Philippe Fauré-Frémiet, quoted in French by Louis Aubert in the sleeve note of the Erato recording (Internet Archive scan): “Entre deux deuils … le luceat eis est tout naturellement murmuré en faveur de ceux qui l’ont bercé”. Translation ours. Fauré’s father died in 1885 and his mother on New Year’s Eve 1887: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Requiem_(Faur%C3%A9)

cues.title: Return of the Introit, Molto largo
cues.text: After a stop, the music resumes at Molto largo. The choir returns to “Requiem aeternam” in D minor, the opening of the whole work, within this movement. The flowing string tune does not return, and low strings hold beneath the voices.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 87–89: fermatas, Molto largo, and the reprise of the Introit in D minor.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the string melody, D major
cues.text: The choir stops. The strings bring back their first melody in D major, a minor third below its original F major. F♯ replaces the F♮ of the Introit, and the organ and pizzicato basses accompany the last phrases.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 90–91: D major, 3/4, returning string melody and pizzicato bass.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: From tenor prayer to full choir
transitions.how: The F major tenor prayer opens into a full choral petition coloured by minor harmony. Violas and cellos continue the moving tune beneath the choir’s changing chords, and bassoons and horns reinforce the voices. The beat stays steady while the choral parts climb and grow louder.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 74–77: the second Agnus Dei petition and its continuing lower-string accompaniment.

transitions.title: Tenor reprise in F major
transitions.how: The full choir makes a diminuendo and stops. The organ plays its opening tune again over a pizzicato bass, and the tenors restate their first melody in F major. Beneath them the violas take over the accompaniment, marked espressivo.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 77–78: diminuendo, organ solo, pizzicato bass and tenor reprise.

transitions.title: C becomes the third of A♭
transitions.to: C · Lux aeterna, opening on held C
transitions.how: The tenor prayer closes in C major. The sopranos hold its keynote alone on “Lux”. At rehearsal E, A♭ enters in the bass and makes that C the third of an A♭ major chord. Altos, divided tenors and divided basses fill out the harmony, pianissimo, and the strings start to move again.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 80–81: C major close, soprano C, and the A♭ major entry at rehearsal E.

transitions.title: Fermatas before the Introit reprise
transitions.from: C · Lux aeterna, opening on held C
transitions.to: D · Introit theme returns, D minor
transitions.how: The strings come to rest on D, and fermatas halt the music. The flowing 3/4 changes to common time and Molto largo. A forceful D fades as the choir enters pianissimo on “Requiem aeternam”. The D minor harmony and slow tempo of the Introit return.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), p. 87: fermatas, change from 3/4 to common time, and Molto largo at the Introit reprise.

transitions.title: D minor opens into D major
transitions.from: D · Introit theme returns, D minor
transitions.to: A″ · Strings alone in D major
transitions.how: F♯ turns the choir’s final chord into D major. The key signature changes to two sharps, the metre returns to 3/4, and the score is marked I° Tempo. Violins and violas take up their flowing melody again over a plucked bass. The choir rests and the instruments play the rest of the movement alone.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 90–91: the change to two sharps and 3/4, I° Tempo, and the instrumental conclusion.

source.title: Fauré, Requiem, Op. 48, full orchestral score (Hamelle, 1901; Kalmus reprint)
source.locator: V. Agnus Dei, printed pp. 70–91: six bars of strings and organ before the tenor entry, Lux aeterna, the Introit’s return and the D major string coda.

timeline.note: Violins and violas play above divided cellos, plucked double basses and organ.
The tenors begin “Agnus Dei”; the violas play their own melody beside them.
Bassoons and horns join the whole choir. Violas and cellos carry the string melody below.
The winds stop as the tenors return with strings and organ.
The sopranos hold C. The other voices enter beneath it in A♭ major, with strings, bassoons, horns and organ.
The music of the Introit returns in D minor, sung by the choir with bassoons, horns, strings and organ.
The choir’s D major chord gives way to the opening string melody.
The strings and organ play the closing bars in D major without the choir.

composer.epithet: Organist and teacher who wrote songs and chamber music in an unusual harmonic language.
facts: École Niedermeyer, 1854–65; Saint-Saëns became his teacher and lifelong friend
Songs, piano music, chamber music, Requiem and the opera Pénélope
composer.background:
As a boy, Fauré often went into the chapel to play the harmonium. His father ran a teachers’ training school at Montgauzy, near Foix, and Gabriel Fauré’s first musical experiences were on the small instrument in its chapel. In October 1854 his father took him to Paris and enrolled him at Louis Niedermeyer’s new school for church musicians. He was nine. For eleven years he studied plainchant, the organ and the polyphony of Renaissance church music.

After Niedermeyer died in 1861, Camille Saint-Saëns took over the piano class. When the official lesson was over, he played the boys Schumann, Liszt and Wagner, composers well outside their syllabus. Saint-Saëns became Fauré’s teacher, champion and friend, and remained so for sixty years. Fauré left school in 1865 with prizes and the Cantique de Jean Racine, a setting of a French prayer over a flowing keyboard part, in which each new choral entry joins a phrase already under way.
